subject: Engineering Materials
summary: crystal structures and defects, phase rule and lever rule, the iron–carbon diagram and its microstructures, TTT diagrams, annealing, normalising, hardening, tempering and surface hardening, and the stress–strain behaviour of metals

questions.text: For the face-centred cubic (FCC) crystal structure, the coordination number and the atomic packing factor are
solution: Concept: Coordination number = number of nearest neighbours; APF = volume of atoms in the cell/cell volume.
FCC has 4 atoms per cell with a = 2√2 r: APF = 4 × (4/3)πr³/(2√2 r)³ = π/(3√2) = 0.74, and each atom touches 12 others.
So the answer is (B) 12 and 0.74. BCC: 8 and 0.68; simple cubic: 6 and 0.52; HCP (ideal): 12 and 0.74.
Exam tip: FCC and HCP are both close-packed (0.74); they differ only in the stacking sequence ABCABC… vs ABAB….

questions.text: Copper has an FCC structure with a lattice parameter of 0.3615 nm. Its atomic radius (in nm, round off to four decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: In FCC the atoms touch along the face diagonal: √2 a = 4r.
Exam tip: In BCC the atoms touch along the body diagonal instead: √3 a = 4r.

questions.text: At the eutectic point of a binary alloy system at constant (atmospheric) pressure, the number of degrees of freedom given by the Gibbs phase rule is
solution: Concept: Gibbs phase rule at constant pressure (condensed systems): F = C − P + 1.
At the eutectic point C = 2 and three phases (L, α, β) coexist: F = 2 − 3 + 1 = 0, answer (C).
The eutectic temperature and the three phase compositions are therefore fixed: the reaction is invariant, which is why the cooling curve shows a thermal arrest.
Exam tip: Eutectic, eutectoid and peritectic points are all invariant (F = 0) in a binary system.

questions.text: Taking the eutectoid composition as 0.76 % C, the carbon content of ferrite as 0.022 % and of cementite as 6.67 %, the mass percentage of ferrite in pearlite (round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: Pearlite is the eutectoid mixture; apply the lever rule across the α + Fe3C tie line at 0.76 % C.
Ferrite = 88.9 %, cementite = 11.1 % (about 8 : 1).
Exam tip: Because ferrite plates are about 8 times as thick as cementite plates, pearlite looks like thin dark lines on a light background.

questions.text: Three invariant points A, B and C are marked on the iron–cementite diagram shown. The reaction that takes place on cooling through point B is
solution: Concept: The Fe–Fe3C diagram has three invariant reactions: peritectic (1493 °C, 0.17 % C), eutectic (1147 °C, 4.3 % C) and eutectoid (727 °C, 0.76 % C).
Point B is at 4.3 % C and 1147 °C, where liquid freezes into austenite and cementite at once: L → γ + Fe<sub>3</sub>C.
The eutectic mixture is called ledeburite: answer (D). A is the peritectic and C the eutectoid (pearlite) point.
Exam tip: Eutectic: liquid → two solids; eutectoid: solid → two solids; peritectic: liquid + solid → another solid.

questions.text: A slowly cooled plain carbon steel is found to contain 30 % pearlite and 70 % proeutectoid ferrite at room temperature. Taking the eutectoid at 0.76 % C and ferrite at 0.022 % C, the carbon content of the steel (in %, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Lever rule just below 727 °C between ferrite (0.022 %) and pearlite (0.76 %).
Exam tip: A quick estimate ignoring the carbon in ferrite is C ≈ 0.76 × (pearlite fraction) = 0.23 %.

questions.text: Compared with a fully annealed specimen of the same hypoeutectoid steel, a normalised specimen has
opts: finer pearlite, a finer grain and higher strength and hardness
less pearlite and more ferrite with the same strength
questions.ans: (B) finer pearlite, a finer grain and higher strength and hardness
solution: Concept: Annealing = furnace cooling from the austenite field; normalising = cooling in still air from about 40 °C above A3 (or Acm).
The faster air cooling lowers the transformation temperature, giving finer pearlite and a finer grain, and also slightly more pearlite (quasi-eutectoid).
Hence higher strength and hardness with good toughness: (B).
Exam tip: Annealing → maximum softness and ductility; normalising → grain refinement and uniform structure (e.g. after forging or casting).

questions.text: The yield strength of a steel obeys the Hall–Petch relation σ<sub>y</sub> = σ<sub>0</sub> + k/√d. It is 250 MPa for a grain size of 16 μm and 190 MPa for a grain size of 64 μm. The yield strength for a grain size of 36 μm (in MPa) is ______
solution: Concept: Two data points fix σ0 and k; then substitute the new grain size.
Exam tip: Grain refinement is the only strengthening mechanism that also improves toughness.

questions.text: The maximum hardness that can be obtained in the martensite of a plain carbon steel depends mainly on
opts: the cooling rate, once it exceeds the critical cooling rate
the carbon content of the steel
questions.ans: (C) the carbon content of the steel
solution: Concept: Martensite hardness comes from the carbon trapped in the BCT lattice.
Once the critical cooling rate is exceeded, cooling faster does not increase hardness; the hardness rises with carbon up to about 0.6–0.8 % C: (C).
Alloying elements raise hardenability (depth of hardening), not the maximum hardness.
Exam tip: Hardness ≠ hardenability: a 0.4 % C alloy steel can harden deeper than a 0.8 % C plain steel, yet be less hard at the surface.

questions.text: A steel has a yield strength of 400 MPa and an elastic modulus of 200 GPa. Its modulus of resilience (in kJ/m³) is ______
solution: Concept: Modulus of resilience = strain energy per unit volume up to the elastic limit = σy2/(2E).
U = 400 kJ/m³
Exam tip: Spring materials need a high σy2/E; toughness (area under the whole curve) is a different property.

questions.text: The TTT diagram of a eutectoid steel is shown with four cooling paths 1–4 (path 4 is held isothermally at 300 °C until transformation is complete). The path that gives a mixture of fine pearlite and martensite is
solution: Concept: A path that misses the start curve gives martensite; one that crosses both start and finish curves gives pearlite; one that crosses only the start curve transforms partly.
Path 2 passes through the nose region between the start and finish curves, so part of the austenite becomes fine pearlite and the rest turns to martensite below Ms: (B).
Path 1 (fastest) → martensite; path 3 (slow) → coarse pearlite; path 4 → lower bainite (austempering).
Exam tip: The critical cooling rate is the slope of the line just touching the nose of the start curve.

questions.text: A cylindrical bar of 12.5 mm diameter and 50 mm gauge length is stretched uniformly (no necking) to a gauge length of 60 mm, the load then being 50 kN. Assuming constant volume, the true stress (in MPa, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: In uniform plastic deformation the volume is constant: A L = A0 L0, and true stress = load/current area.
σtrue = 50 000/102.27 = 488.9 MPa (engineering stress 407.4 MPa; σtrue = σeng(1 + e) = 407.4 × 1.2).
Exam tip: The true strain here is ln(60/50) = 0.182, smaller than the engineering strain 0.2.

questions.text: Which one of the following is a planar (two-dimensional) crystal defect?
solution: Concept: Defects are classified by dimension.

Point (0-D): vacancies, interstitial and substitutional atoms. Line (1-D): edge and screw dislocations. Planar (2-D): grain boundaries, twin boundaries, stacking faults, free surfaces. Volume (3-D): voids, inclusions.
Answer: (D) grain boundary.
Exam tip: Plastic deformation in metals takes place by the motion of dislocations (line defects).

questions.text: Aluminium is FCC with a lattice parameter of 0.405 nm. The interplanar spacing of its (111) planes (in nm, round off to four decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: For cubic crystals dhkl = a/√(h² + k² + l²).
Exam tip: The (111) planes are the most widely spaced (close-packed) planes in FCC, which is why slip occurs on them.

questions.text: For a eutectoid steel, the microconstituents arranged in decreasing order of hardness are
opts: martensite, bainite, fine pearlite, coarse pearlite, spheroidite
bainite, martensite, coarse pearlite, fine pearlite, spheroidite
martensite, fine pearlite, bainite, spheroidite, coarse pearlite
spheroidite, coarse pearlite, fine pearlite, bainite, martensite
questions.ans: (A) martensite, bainite, fine pearlite, coarse pearlite, spheroidite
solution: Concept: Hardness rises as the carbide becomes finer and as carbon is trapped in the iron lattice.
Martensite (supersaturated BCT) is the hardest; bainite has very fine carbides; fine pearlite has thinner lamellae than coarse pearlite; spheroidite (globular carbides) is the softest.
Answer: (A). Ductility follows the reverse order.
Exam tip: Spheroidising is used on high-carbon steels to give the best machinability and cold formability.
